title: Best CPU Cooler for Ryzen 5 9600X (2026): 5 Picks Under $55
description: An $18–$25 Thermalright Assassin X 120 Refined SE is enough for a 65 W Ryzen 5 9600X. For 105 W mode or a 7600X, a $35 dual tower. 5 picks under $55.
dek: The 9600X ships without a cooler and runs at 65 W by default. That makes it one of the cheapest current chips to cool well.
intro: The Thermalright Assassin X 120 Refined SE is the best cooler for most Ryzen 5 9600X builds. AMD rates the 9600X at 65 W by default, and this $18 to $25 single tower with four heat pipes handles that easily, keeping the cooler at about a tenth of a $190 to $230 processor.

This guide is for anyone buying a 9600X, which comes without a cooler in the box, and for Ryzen 5 7600X owners, since the two chips need the same class of cooler once you account for power modes. We cover the 9600X's optional 105 W mode, whether an old Wraith cooler will do, and when a dual tower is worth the extra $15.
quickAnswer: For a stock 65 W 9600X, buy the Thermalright Assassin X 120 Refined SE ($18–$25). If you enable the 105 W mode or own a 7600X, step up to the Peerless Assassin 120 SE or Phantom Spirit 120 SE ($35–$45). The Arctic Freezer 36 ($30–$40) is the quiet single-tower option, and the Noctua NH-U12S redux ($45–$55) adds a 6-year warranty.

picks.label: Best Overall
picks.bestFor: a stock 65 W Ryzen 5 9600X gaming build
picks.skipIf: you plan to run the 105 W mode with long all-core workloads
writeup: The 9600X is a six-core chip that AMD ships in a 65 W mode, and at that setting it is easy to cool. The Assassin X 120 Refined SE has four 6 mm heat pipes and one 120 mm fan, which is more than the chip needs in games and enough for its 88 W stock package limit in all-core work.

The price is the reason it ranks first. A $200 processor does not need a $45 cooler at stock, and the $20 or so saved goes straight to the graphics card, which sets the frame rate on a six-core gaming PC. Owners pairing budget Thermalright single towers with 65 W Ryzen chips commonly report quiet operation in games.

At 148 mm it is short enough for most compact mid-towers and, as a single tower, it never covers the memory slots, so any DDR5 kit fits. It mounts into the stock AM5 backplate. If you later turn on the 105 W mode for rendering, it still runs the chip, just with a louder fan; that is the point to consider a dual tower.
cons: Single fan gets loud at 105 W

picks.label: Best for 105 W Mode
picks.bestFor: 9600X owners who enable 105 W mode, and Ryzen 5 7600X builds
picks.skipIf: you leave the 9600X at stock 65 W and only game
writeup: AMD added an optional 105 W mode for the 9600X through a BIOS update. It raises the package power limit to about 142 W, the same as a Ryzen 5 7600X, and mainly speeds up multi-thread work; independent reviews found game gains small. If you plan to use it, a dual tower keeps the fans calm.

The Peerless Assassin 120 SE is the dual tower to buy at this level. Six heat pipes and two 120 mm fans handle 142 W comfortably, so a long render or compile runs without the fan racing. It is the same pick we would make for a 7600X, which uses that power by default.

It costs $35 to $45, stands 155 mm tall and mounts into the stock AM5 backplate. The front fan overhangs the first DIMM slot, so low-profile DDR5 is the easy match; tall RGB kits may need the fan raised a few millimeters.

picks.label: Quietest Single Tower
picks.bestFor: quiet 9600X builds and anyone with tall RGB memory
picks.skipIf: you want the most all-core headroom for the money
writeup: The Freezer 36 adds a second fan to the single-tower formula. Its two P12 Pressure-optimised fans run in push-pull across four heat pipes, so for the same heat they can turn slower than a single-fan cooler. On a 65 W 9600X that means a PC that is close to silent in games.

Because it is a single tower, it sits behind the memory rather than over it, so tall RGB DDR5 fits without adjustment. It also handles the 105 W mode at reasonable noise, though the Thermalright dual towers have more capacity for long all-core jobs.

It costs $30 to $40 and stands 159 mm tall. Arctic sells standard, A-RGB and CO versions; the CO uses dual ball bearing fans, a sensible choice for a 9600X that runs a home server or stays on around the clock.

picks.label: Best Warranty
picks.bestFor: buyers who want Noctua's mounting system and a 6-year warranty on a budget build
picks.skipIf: you want the best cooling per dollar
writeup: The NH-U12S redux is the most expensive cooler on this list and the least necessary, but it earns a place for buyers who keep a PC for many years. Noctua's 6-year warranty and SecuFirm2 mounting are well regarded, and it moves to later AM5 chips without new hardware.

Four heat pipes and one NF-P12 redux fan handle a 65 W 9600X easily, and the 105 W mode at moderate noise. On cooling per dollar it trails the Freezer 36 and the Thermalright towers, so the extra $10 to $30 buys support and build quality rather than temperatures.
It is 158 mm tall in a slim tower that clears the memory slots. If you value a quiet, low-maintenance cooler from a company with a long support record, it is a reasonable spend on a budget AM5 build.

picks.label: Best for an X3D Upgrade
picks.bestFor: 9600X owners planning to move to a 9800X3D or later Ryzen on the same board
picks.skipIf: you expect to keep the 9600X for the life of the PC
writeup: The 9600X is a common starting point for an AM5 build that later takes an X3D chip, and AMD has said AM5 will be supported through at least 2027. If that is your plan, the Phantom Spirit 120 SE is the cooler to buy once.

Its seven heat pipes are far more than a 9600X needs, but they comfortably cover a 120 W 9800X3D, which is where the extra capacity pays off. Buying it now avoids a second cooler purchase and a second mounting job when you swap processors; see our [9800X3D cooler guide](/best-cpu-cooler-for-ryzen-7-9800x3d/) for how it fares on that chip.

It costs $35 to $45, the same as the Peerless Assassin, and stands 154 mm tall with the same front-fan overhang on the first memory slot. For a 9600X alone it is overkill; for a 9600X now and an X3D chip later, it is the efficient choice.

ranking.intro: We ranked these coolers for the Ryzen 5 9600X using AMD's published specs, cooler makers' spec sheets, independent reviews of the CPU and the coolers, and AM5 owner reports. None of these coolers were bench-tested by us. The ER Score weighs that evidence against price and fit for a 65 W six-core chip, which favors cheap single towers more than our general cooler guide does.
criteria: Whether the cooler handles the 9600X's default 88 W package limit quietly.
How it copes with the optional 142 W limit, the same as a Ryzen 5 7600X.
The cooler should cost a small share of a budget processor.
Height, AM5 mounting in the box, and overhang over the first DIMM slot.
Fan quality, warranty length and whether it suits a later AM5 upgrade.
ranking.why: The Assassin X 120 Refined SE won because it cools a stock 9600X quietly for about $20, the right spend for a 65 W chip.

mentions.text: An excellent AIO, but $85–$110 of liquid cooling on a 65 W six-core chip is money that would do more in the graphics card. It only makes sense if the 9600X is a placeholder for a 16-core Ryzen.
Noctua's flagship air cooler is far beyond what a 9600X needs, even in the 105 W mode. At $140–$160 it can cost three-quarters of the CPU. Buy it for a 16-core chip, not this one.

mentions.name: AMD Wraith Stealth
mentions.text: AMD's small stock cooler ships with the Ryzen 5 7600, not the 9600X. If you own one, it can run a 9600X at 65 W, but it is louder under load and not suited to the 105 W mode. A $20 tower is a worthwhile upgrade.

sections.h: Does the Ryzen 5 9600X Come With a Cooler?
body: No. AMD sells the Ryzen 5 9600X without a cooler, so you need to add one to the budget. The cheaper non-X Ryzen 5 7600 includes AMD's Wraith Stealth, which is part of why the 7600 remains popular for budget builds; compare the two in our [Ryzen 5 9600X vs Ryzen 5 7600](/compare/ryzen-5-9600x-vs-ryzen-5-7600/) page.
The good news is that the 9600X's cooler can be cheap. At its default 65 W, an $18 to $25 single tower is enough, so the total for CPU plus cooler stays around $210 to $255.

sections.h: How Much Cooling Does a 65 W 9600X Need?
body: Very little. At 65 W TDP, the 9600X's package power limit on AM5 is 88 W, and in games it draws less than that. A four-heat-pipe single tower handles it with a quiet fan, and even AMD's small Wraith Stealth can keep it within limits, though more loudly.

The chip's maximum operating temperature is 95°C, and Precision Boost raises clocks until it reaches either the power limit or that temperature. With any cooler on this list at 65 W, the power limit is reached first, so a bigger cooler adds almost nothing at stock.

sections.h: Should You Turn On the 9600X's 105 W Mode?
body: Only if you do a lot of multi-thread work. AMD's optional 105 W mode, enabled in a BIOS that supports it, lifts the package limit to about 142 W. Independent reviews found it speeds up rendering and compiling noticeably, while games gain little, because they rarely load all six cores to the limit.
If you enable it, plan for a dual tower. The chip then behaves much like a Ryzen 5 7600X, and a $35 to $45 dual tower keeps it quiet under long loads.

sections.h: Does the Same Cooler Work for the Ryzen 5 7600X?
body: Yes, with one adjustment. The 7600X is rated at 105 W, so it runs at the same 142 W package limit the 9600X uses in its 105 W mode. That makes a dual tower like the Peerless Assassin 120 SE the better default for a 7600X, while a single tower is still fine for gaming.

Like the 9600X, the 7600X ships without a cooler, uses the same AM5 mounting and lists the same 95°C maximum temperature. If you move from a 7600X to a 9600X later, your cooler moves with it. The eight-core Ryzen 7 9700X shares the same power modes; see our [best CPU cooler for Ryzen 7 9700X](/best-cpu-cooler-for-ryzen-7-9700x/) guide.

sections.h: Will an Old AM4 or Wraith Cooler Work on the 9600X?
body: Usually. AM5 kept AM4's cooler mounting holes, so coolers that bolt into AMD's stock backplate fit a 9600X. Coolers that need their own backplate require an AM5 kit from the maker, and you should never remove the AM5 backplate, which holds the socket.

A Wraith Stealth or Wraith Spire from an older Ryzen will run a 65 W 9600X, but expect more fan noise in long loads, and do not pair either with the 105 W mode. A $20 to $40 tower is one of the cheapest noticeable upgrades in a budget build.

sections.h: How Much Should You Spend on a 9600X Cooler?
body: About $20 to $45. Under $20 you are into unbranded coolers with unknown fans; over $45 you are paying for quiet, looks or a future CPU, not for the 9600X. For a gaming-only build, the low end of that range is the right call.
Put any savings into the graphics card or memory. A six-core 9600X is usually GPU-limited at 1440p, so an extra $25 on the GPU does more for frame rates than any cooler upgrade.

mistakes: Buying an AIO for a 65 W chip
A liquid cooler on a stock 9600X adds cost, a pump and a failure point without improving gaming performance. The chip reaches its power limit long before its temperature limit on a $20 tower.
Forgetting the cooler is not in the box
The 9600X ships without a cooler, unlike the Ryzen 5 7600. Order one with the CPU, or the build will stall on day one. Budget $20 to $45.
Enabling 105 W mode on a stock-style cooler

The optional 105 W mode lifts the package limit to about 142 W. On a Wraith Stealth or a small single tower that means loud fans and earlier throttling. Pair it with a dual tower, or leave the chip at 65 W.

AM5's heat spreader has notches around the edges that trap excess paste. A pea-sized dot in the center spreads well under pressure. More paste does not cool better and makes the next CPU swap messier.
bottomLine: The Ryzen 5 9600X is cheap to cool. At its default 65 W, the $18 to $25 Thermalright Assassin X 120 Refined SE is all it needs, and the Arctic Freezer 36 is the quieter single-tower option. If you enable the 105 W mode or own a 7600X, buy the Peerless Assassin 120 SE, and choose the Phantom Spirit 120 SE if you plan to move to an X3D chip later.

faqs.q: Does the Ryzen 5 9600X need a good cooler?
faqs.a: Not an expensive one. At its default 65 W, the 9600X runs well on an $18 to $25 single-tower cooler like the Thermalright Assassin X 120 Refined SE. Spend more only for the 105 W mode, lower noise, or a planned upgrade to a hotter AM5 chip.

faqs.q: What is the maximum temperature for a Ryzen 5 9600X?
faqs.a: AMD lists 95°C as the maximum operating temperature for the 9600X. The chip boosts until it reaches its power or temperature limit. At 65 W with any decent cooler, it hits the power limit first and runs well below 95°C in games.

faqs.q: Can I use the Wraith Stealth on a 9600X?
faqs.a: Yes, at the default 65 W, but it is louder than an aftermarket tower under load and not suited to the 105 W mode. The Wraith Stealth ships with the Ryzen 5 7600, not the 9600X. A $20 tower is a worthwhile upgrade.

faqs.q: What is the best cooler for the Ryzen 5 7600X?
faqs.a: A dual tower like the Thermalright Peerless Assassin 120 SE ($35–$45). The 7600X is rated at 105 W with a 142 W package limit, so it benefits from more capacity than a 65 W 9600X. A single tower is still fine if you only game.

faqs.q: Is the 9600X's 105 W mode worth it?
faqs.a: For multi-thread work, yes; for gaming, rarely. Reviews found it speeds up rendering and compiling while game frame rates barely change. If you enable it, use a dual-tower cooler so the extra power does not mean extra fan noise.

faqs.q: Is a liquid cooler good for a 9600X?
faqs.a: It works, but it is poor value. A 240 mm or 360 mm AIO costs $70 to $110 and does not raise gaming performance on a 65 W six-core chip. Choose one only for looks, or if the 9600X is a stopgap before a 16-core Ryzen.

No more than other Ryzen 9000 chips at its power. At 65 W it is one of the cooler-running current CPUs. Short temperature spikes when a core wakes are normal on Ryzen and do not mean your cooler is failing; smooth the fan curve to ignore them.

faqs.q: Will my 9600X cooler fit a future AM5 CPU?
faqs.a: Yes. AM5 keeps the same cooler mounting between generations, so any cooler here moves to a later Ryzen. If you plan to upgrade to a 9800X3D or a 12- to 16-core chip, buy a seven-pipe dual tower like the Phantom Spirit 120 SE now.
